record.paper_title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials: perspectives and open questions
record.original_question: What role do elastic interactions between Eshelby quadrupoles play in shear-band formation, and can a self-consistent nonlinear theory of quadrupolar and dipolar interactions determine the intensity, density, and organization of quadrupoles that create a shear band in amorphous solids?

evidence.quote: The identification of these effects leaves open the question of the role of elastic interactions between Eshelby quadrupoles in the formation of shear bands.

Expanding this theory to address instabilities and shear banding necessitates further development, specifically including nonlinear quadrupolar and dipolar interactions. This ongoing work holds the potential to allow a self-consistent determination of the intensity and density of quadrupoles that are involved in creating the shear band.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider an amorphous solid (a disordered, non-crystalline elastic medium) undergoing quasi-static shear deformation. Local plastic rearrangements in such a medium are modeled as Eshelby inclusions, whose far-field displacement is that of an elastic quadrupole; spatial gradients of a non-uniform quadrupolar density act as elastic dipoles, producing screening effects and emergent characteristic length scales beyond classical elasticity.

(a) Determine the role played by the elastic interactions between Eshelby quadrupoles in the formation of macroscopic shear bands. In particular, identify how pairwise (and higher-order) quadrupole–quadrupole couplings, together with the induced dipolar fields, drive the localization of plastic activity into a band.

(b) Develop a self-consistent nonlinear continuum theory that simultaneously incorporates nonlinear quadrupolar and dipolar interactions, and use it to predict from first principles the following quantities characterizing a shear band that forms under an applied shear:
  (i) the intensity (amplitude) of the quadrupoles populating the band,
  (ii) their spatial number density inside the band, and
  (iii) their geometric organization (orientation, alignment, and spatial arrangement).

The goal is a closed, self-consistent set of equations whose solutions yield the intensity, density, and organization of quadrupoles that produce a shear band in an amorphous solid.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent work has developed an analytic nonlinear theory of shear banding in amorphous solids using quadrupolar and dipolar fields, including a weakly nonlinear amplitude equation that predicts shear-band width in terms of elastic moduli, and an elastic criterion for the shear-banding instability. These works represent substantial progress toward a self-consistent quadrupolar/dipolar theory, but a fully self-consistent determination of the intensity, density, and organization of quadrupoles forming a shear band is still under active development.

status_evidence.title: Analytic Nonlinear Theory of Shear Banding in Amorphous Solids
status_evidence.snippet: Nonlinear theory exposes an instability resulting in shear bands; weakly nonlinear amplitude equation yields analytic expressions for displacement fields and shear band width.
status_evidence.claim: A nonlinear quadrupolar/dipolar theory of shear banding has been partially developed, but extensions toward a fully self-consistent description of quadrupole intensity, density, and organization are still in progress.

status_evidence.title: Elastic criterion for shear-banding instability in amorphous solids
status_evidence.snippet: Provides an elastic criterion for the shear-banding instability based on quadrupolar plastic events.
status_evidence.claim: An elastic criterion derived from quadrupolar plastic events has been proposed, contributing to but not completing a self-consistent theory.

status_evidence.title: Eshelby-inclusion characteristics of shear rearrangements in amorphous solids
status_evidence.snippet: Characterizes Eshelby-inclusion features of plastic rearrangements in amorphous solids.
status_evidence.claim: Quantitative characterization of Eshelby quadrupoles supports ongoing efforts to build a self-consistent theory.
